To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dystrophin-deficiency causes muscle fibers to fail in the absence of electrical stimulation, that this failure is due to an influx of Ca(2+)(extracellular) into the fibers, and that the failure is due to a combination of the membrane stabilization function and the mechanical coupling function of dystrophin.

dystrophin-deficiency results in a failure cascade that is initiated by stress-induced entry of extracellular calcium, causing localized activation to persist in dystrophic muscles following cessation of stimulation and proceeding as persistent local activation results in the separation of myoplsm in nonactivated regions.

dystrophin-deficiency causes muscle fibers to fail in response to stress by a mechanism that involves a stress-induced influx and persistent localization of calcium, and the failure cascade proceeds as the persistent calcium activation, combined with the reduced lateral mechanical coupling of the contractile core to the extracellular matrix that results from dystrophin's absence, causes the longitudinal separation of the fiber myoplasm.
